title: Give & receive I: あげる・くれる・もらう (things)

grammarPoints.rule: English has one verb for this and Japanese has three, so the first thing to do is stop looking for the word that means give. There isn't one. What Japanese has instead is three verbs that all describe the same event — a thing leaving one person and arriving at another — and which one you reach for depends on WHICH WAY it moved past you. Not on who is talking. Not on politeness. On direction. Start with the one that points away. あげる is what you say when something leaves your side of the line and goes to somebody on the other side of it. 「ともだちに プレゼントを あげる。」 I'll give my friend a present. The sentence itself is nothing new: the giver takes は, the person who gets it takes に, the thing takes を, and the verb comes last, exactly as it has since module 4. The only new thing in it is あげる. Now the line, because everything in this module hangs off it. Japanese draws a circle around you and the people who belong to you — your family, and by extension anyone you are speaking for — and everybody else stands outside it. Japanese has names for the two sides, うち and そと, inside and outside. あげる measures that circle: it is the verb for a thing going OUT. So 「ははは せんせいに はなを あげる。」 works, because my mother is inside and the teacher is outside. And that is already enough to tell you the thing あげる cannot do, which is the whole of lesson seven: it can never point back in at you.

examples.en: I'll give my friend a present.

antiPattern.ja: ともだちに プレゼントを もらう。
antiPattern.why: もらう is the verb for something coming TO the subject, so this says I get a present from my friend — the opposite event. Something you hand over takes あげる: ともだちに プレゼントを あげる。

grammarPoints.rule: Same present, same friend, same afternoon — and a different verb, because now the thing is coming the other way. くれる is あげる pointed back at you. Something leaves somebody OUTSIDE your circle and arrives INSIDE it. 「ともだちが プレゼントを くれる。」 My friend gives me a present. Look hard at what changed and what did not. The thing still takes を. The verb still comes last. What moved is the direction, and one small thing you may not have noticed: the giver here is marked が rather than は, and the receiver — me — is not in the sentence at all. Both of those are the same fact. くれる already says the thing came to my side, so saying わたしに as well is like saying I myself personally: not wrong, just unnecessary, and Japanese leaves out what it has already said. Lesson eleven is about exactly that disappearance. This is the pair worth burning in, because it is the one English speakers get wrong for years. あげる and くれる are not two levels of politeness and they are not giver-verb and receiver-verb. They are ONE EVENT DESCRIBED FROM OPPOSITE ENDS. If you can see the present travelling, あげる is you watching it leave and くれる is you watching it arrive. Everything else in this module is a consequence of that.

antiPattern.ja: ともだちが プレゼントを あげる。
antiPattern.why: あげる cannot bring something to your own side, so this sentence never arrives anywhere — a thing coming in from outside takes くれる: ともだちが プレゼントを くれる。

grammarPoints.rule: You have known に since module 5 and every に you have met so far has been a place. 「がっこうに いく。」 「うちに かえる。」 に marks where something ENDS UP. This module hands it a person, and once you see that it is the same job you will never have to learn it twice: 「ともだちに はなたばを あげる。」 The bouquet ends up at my friend, so my friend takes に. A transfer is a journey with a person at the far end of it, and Japanese marks the far end the same way whether it is a station or a sister. So the full shape of an あげる sentence is three slots and a verb, and you already own all four: WHO GIVES takes は, WHO GETS takes に, WHAT MOVES takes を, verb last. 「あねは せんせいに てがみを あげる。」 The one thing worth practising is the order, because English does it two ways — I gave my friend a book, I gave a book to my friend — and Japanese only does it one. Person before thing is the ordinary order. And because every slot is labelled by its particle rather than by its position, you can ask about any one of them with だれ: 「だれに あげる？」 Who are you giving it to? The particle stays put and the question word drops into the slot.

examples.ja: ともだちに はなたばを あげる。
examples.en: I'll give my friend a bouquet.

examples.ja: あねは せんせいに てがみを あげる。
examples.en: My older sister gives the teacher a letter.

examples.ja: だれに おみやげを あげる？

antiPattern.ja: ともだちを はなたばに あげる。
antiPattern.why: を marks the thing that moves and に marks the person it reaches — swapping them hands a friend over to a bouquet: ともだちに はなたばを あげる。

grammarPoints.rule: Third verb, and it is the one that rearranges the sentence rather than just pointing it. もらう means to get, to receive — and the subject of もらう is the person who ENDS UP HOLDING THE THING. 「せんせいに じしょを もらう。」 I get a dictionary from the teacher. Compare that with くれる, because they report the identical event: 「せんせいが じしょを くれる」 and 「せんせいに じしょを もらう」 describe one dictionary changing hands once. What differs is who the sentence is ABOUT. くれる is about the teacher and what the teacher did; もらう is about me and what I ended up with. Now the part that catches everybody. The person the thing came FROM takes に — the same に, doing a job that feels backwards. With あげる, に pointed at the person the thing was going to. With もらう, に points at the person it came from. That is not two rules: に marks the OTHER PERSON in the transfer, and the verb decides which end that person is standing at. English does the same trick with a different word and nobody blinks — you give TO somebody, you hear it FROM somebody — Japanese just declines to change the particle. One practical note. Because もらう is about the receiver, it is the natural verb the moment you want to say what YOU got, and it is what you will actually use most.

examples.ja: せんせいに じしょを もらう。
examples.en: I get a dictionary from the teacher.

examples.ja: たんじょうびに ちちに とけいを もらう。

examples.ja: いしゃに くすりを もらう。

examples.ja: あねは ともだちに おみやげを もらう。

examples.ja: かいしゃの ひとに おかしを もらう。
examples.en: I get sweets from the people at the company.

antiPattern.ja: せんせいは じしょを もらう。
antiPattern.why: the subject of もらう is whoever ends up holding the thing, so this says the TEACHER is the one who got a dictionary — if you are the one who received it, you are the subject: せんせいに じしょを もらう。

grammarPoints.rule: もらう is the one place in this module where Japanese lets you choose, and it is worth knowing that the choice is real rather than a trap. The person a thing came from can be marked に or から, and both are correct: 「ともだちに おみやげを もらう。」 「ともだちから おみやげを もらう。」 Nobody will correct either one. から is module 4's word and it has always meant the starting point — 「にほんから きた」, came from Japan — so all that has happened is that a person is now allowed to be a starting point. に is the tighter, more ordinary choice and it is what you will hear most in speech. から is slightly more explicit about the source, and it is what people reach for when the giver is an organisation rather than a person, or when the sentence is long enough that an extra に would be one に too many. There is one case where から is not a preference but the answer, and it is worth having: when the source is not a person at all. 「かいしゃから きねんの とけいを もらう。」 A company is a place as much as a giver, and に in that sentence starts to read as a destination. Notice also that this choice belongs to もらう alone. あげる and くれる have no source slot to mark, so から never appears with them — which makes から a quiet signal, when you are listening, that もらう is coming.

examples.ja: ともだちから おみやげを もらう。
examples.en: I get a souvenir from my friend.

examples.ja: かいしゃから きねんの とけいを もらう。
examples.en: I get a commemorative watch from the company.

examples.ja: せんせいから おいわいの カードを もらう。

examples.ja: がくせいから てがみを もらう。

examples.ja: こんど いしゃから くすりを もらう。

antiPattern.ja: ともだちから プレゼントを あげる。
antiPattern.why: から marks where a thing came from and あげる has no source slot — only もらう can take a から: ともだちから プレゼントを もらう。

grammarPoints.rule: Here is the ban, and it is the one thing in this module that is not a preference. あげる CANNOT POINT AT YOU. 「わたしに プレゼントを あげる」 is not awkward, not childish, not impolite — it is broken, in the way that I gave me a present is broken in English, and a Japanese speaker will not be able to work out what you meant. The reason is the same one that has been running the whole module. あげる's arrow leaves your circle. There is nowhere for it to land if the destination is inside the circle it just left. So the moment the thing is arriving at you, あげる is off the table and you have exactly two verbs to choose from — and which one you use is not about the event, it is about what you want the sentence to be ABOUT. くれる if the giver is the news: 「ともだちが プレゼントを くれる。」 もらう if what you ended up with is the news: 「ともだちに プレゼントを もらう。」 Both are right, both are ordinary, and swapping them changes nothing but the emphasis. The circle stretches, too, and this is the part that takes practice. Your family is inside it. 「ともだちが いもうとに おかしを くれる」 is fine, because the sweets came in to my side of the line even though they did not come to my hand. Say あげる there and you have pushed your own sister outside the circle, which is a stranger thing to say than any particle mistake.

examples.ja: ともだちが わたしに プレゼントを くれる。
examples.en: My friend gives me a present.

examples.ja: ともだちに プレゼントを もらう。
examples.en: I get a present from my friend.

examples.ja: せんせいが いもうとに おかしを くれる。

examples.ja: がくせいに ノートを あげる。

examples.ja: ともだちが ケーキを くれるから うれしい。
examples.en: My friend is giving me a cake, so I'm happy.

antiPattern.ja: ともだちが わたしに プレゼントを あげる。
antiPattern.why: あげる's arrow leaves your side and can never land back on you — a thing arriving at you takes くれる: ともだちが わたしに プレゼントを くれる。

grammarPoints.rule: Everything so far has been about presents that have not been handed over yet. Put the three verbs in the past and the module becomes usable, because most of what anybody says about a gift is said afterwards. The forms are module 11's and nothing about them is new. あげる and くれる are る-verbs: drop る, add た. あげた. くれた. もらう is an う-verb ending in う, so it takes the same った row かう does: もらった. That is it — no sound change to memorise that you have not already met. What IS worth watching is that the direction does not soften in the past. 「ともだちが けいたいを くれた」 still points in at me; 「ともだちに けいたいを あげた」 still points out. Learners who have got the pair straight in the non-past sometimes lose it in the past, because the English translation collapses again — gave, for both. Say the arrow to yourself before you pick the verb. One more thing you get for free. 「もらった」 is the single most useful of the three, because it is how you answer the question the past tense invites. 「その とけい、いいね。」 「たんじょうびに ちちに もらった。」 Nice watch. My father gave it to me for my birthday — except that the Japanese says I got it from my father, which is the same news told from the end that matters.

examples.ja: たんじょうびに ちちに とけいを もらった。
examples.en: I got a watch from my father for my birthday.

examples.ja: ともだちが けいたいを くれた。
examples.en: My friend gave me a mobile phone.

examples.ja: せんせいに はなたばを あげた。
examples.en: I gave the teacher a bouquet.

examples.ja: プレゼントを もらったから うれしかった。

examples.ja: いしゃに くすりを もらったから あした がっこうに いく。
examples.en: I got medicine from the doctor, so I'll go to school tomorrow.

antiPattern.ja: たんじょうびに ちちに とけいを あげった。
antiPattern.why: あげる is a る-verb, so its past is あげた — った belongs to う-verbs like もらう: たんじょうびに ちちに とけいを もらった。

grammarPoints.rule: Two more words, and for now you only have to RECOGNISE them. When the person giving is somebody you look up to — a teacher, a customer, somebody much older — Japanese swaps the verb rather than adding a polite ending. くれる becomes くださる, and もらう becomes いただく. 「せんせいが じしょを くださった。」 The teacher was kind enough to give me a dictionary. 「せんせいに じしょを いただいた。」 I received a dictionary from the teacher. Notice that the axis has not moved an inch. くださる points in at me exactly like くれる, and いただく makes the receiver the subject exactly like もらう. The direction system you have just learned is doing all the work; what has been added is a layer of respect sitting on top of it, which is why the spine teaches direction first and respect much later. So why meet them now at all? Because you will hear them constantly and they do not look like their plain partners — you cannot get to くださった from くれる by any rule you own. Recognising them is worth having today. Producing them is not: くださる in particular has an irregular polite form that trips native learners of the language too, and this course teaches it properly at module 50 rather than badly now. Until then, when you are the one speaking, use くれる and もらう. Nobody will think you rude.

examples.ja: せんせいが じしょを くださった。
examples.en: The teacher was kind enough to give me a dictionary.

examples.ja: せんせいに じしょを いただいた。
examples.en: I received a dictionary from the teacher.

examples.ja: たなかさんが おいわいの はなたばを くださる。
examples.en: Tanaka is kind enough to give me a congratulatory bouquet.

examples.ja: かいしゃから きねんの カードを いただく。
examples.en: I receive a commemorative card from the company.

examples.ja: しんせつな せんせいに ノートを もらった。
examples.en: I got a notebook from a kind teacher.

antiPattern.ja: ともだちが おかしを くださった。
antiPattern.why: くださる is for somebody you look up to, so using it of a friend puts a stranger between you — a friend takes くれる: ともだちが おかしを くれた。

grammarPoints.rule: Last piece, and it is the one that makes the module pay. Because くれる and もらう already say which way the thing moved, Japanese stops mentioning you. 「ともだちが けいたいを くれた。」 There is no わたしに in that sentence and there does not need to be — くれる cannot point anywhere else. Same with もらう: 「ちちに おかねを もらった」 has no わたしは in it, because the subject of もらう is whoever is speaking unless somebody else is named. This is not laziness and it is not an abbreviation of a longer sentence. It is the payoff for having a direction built into the verb: the verb has already told you who, so saying it again would be repeating yourself. And it works the other way round, which is how you use it deliberately. If you DO put わたしは or わたしに in, you are contrasting — 「わたしは かさを もらった」 lands as I got an umbrella, whatever everyone else got. That is module 3's は doing its oldest job, marking a topic against a background. So the practical rule for listening is: when a sentence has くれる in it and no receiver, the receiver is the speaker or somebody on the speaker's side. When it has もらう and no subject, the subject is the speaker. And when the speaker DOES say わたし, listen for what they are setting themselves against, because they had no other reason to say it.

examples.en: My friend gave me a mobile phone.

examples.ja: ちちに おかねを もらった。
examples.en: I got money from my father.

antiPattern.why: くれる is what carries a thing to your side, and it carries it without needing わたしに at all: ともだちが けいたいを くれた。

beats.stem: びょうきの ときに ともだちが くだものを
beats.answer: くれた
beats.en: When I was ill my friend gave me some fruit
beats.explanation: the fruit came to me while I was ill, so くれる is the verb and it has already happened. あげた would send it to my friend, and かりた would mean I have to give it back.
